The work is cited in various publications, including *Sämmtliche Werke* (edited by Suphan and Abeken), *Goethe-Jahrbuch* (1893, pages 51–52), and *Jahresberichte für neuere deutsche Literaturgeschichte* (1893, page 106).

The phrase "Die harten Schattirungen meines Gewebes" refers to harsh shading in the fabric of the author's work, indicating a stark or intense visual or emotional texture. This characteristic is directly associated with the textile, as the harsh shading is a feature present in the textile. The description highlights the visual intensity of the textile's appearance, suggesting a deliberate use of contrast or depth in its design.

"Reisen des grünen Mannes durch Deutschland," published in Halle between 1787 and 1791, is an imitation of Jean Paul and is indirectly connected with Yorick. It is referenced in footnote 24, which also cites "Bemerkungen oder Briefe über Wien" (Leipzig, 1804 or 1805), containing extravagant sentiment directed toward "Evelina," and "Meine Reise vom Städtchen H" (Hannover, 1799), as well as "Reisen unter Sonne, Mond und Sternen" (Erfurt, 1798, p. 220, 8vo). A profusely annotated edition of a "Sentimental Journey" was published in Halle in 1794, considered not to be read but studied by an anonymous editor. Another annotated edition, "A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy," was also published in Halle in 1794 by Renger, with annotations and a word index. Halle is associated with a publication period from 1767 to 1771 and with Carl Heine’s work "Der Roman in Deutschland von 1774 bis 1778," published in Halle in 1892.

Eighteenth-century German novels were marked by defects stemming from the peculiar mental organization of German authorship, suppressed by pedantry and pedagogy. German culture has an inborn need to impart information, recruit supporters, and promote political, educational, and moral theories, leading novelists—seen as men of mind rather than action—to emphasize reflection, abstraction, theory, and inner life. Hillebrand identifies the root cause as a "tutorial attitude," stating "we are all schoolmasters," and Hettner highlights the introduction to *Sebaldus Nothanker* as a representative example. Goethe, in a letter to Zelter dated October 5, 1830, and in a conversation reported by Riemer, expressed admiration for Sterne, who he believed raised both himself and others from pedantry and philistinism, particularly through a "gay arraignment" of these traits. The conversation of ladies A, B, C, D in the last chapter exhibits typographical eccentricity.

The *Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen* published on October 3 and 6, 1775, praised Bode’s translation of the *Briefe an Elisa*, affirming its authenticity and highlighting Sterne’s observation on fragile obstacles to desire. The Yorick character’s love is exalted above Swift’s, Waller’s, and Scarron’s, with his godly fear balancing explicit dishonoring desire. The anonymous 1772 Hamburg work *Zween Tage eines Schwindsüchtigen, etwas Empfindsames*, a free revision of *Das lustige und lächerliche Lalenburg*, is noted by Hillebrand as an extreme example of absurd sentimental tendency based on its title, though it is actually merely thoughtful and contemplative. The *Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen* later references the work, disagreeing with the view that it does not exemplify the author’s theories and instead considers it a genuine example. Goethe criticized the second volume of Schummel’s work in the *Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen* on March 3, 1772.

Erich Schmidt, in his 1884 edition of Lessing's life, claimed a connection between Just’s dog and Sterne’s Trim, stating the similarity in the motif of animal fidelity is pure coincidence, and that Just’s dog serves as a forceful, immediate comparison rather than for humanitarian or sentimental contrast. Schmidt corrected this claim in 1899, based on Paul Albrecht’s work, which is considered unreliable due to its absurdity and violent attacks, despite occasional genuine discoveries. The 1884 edition includes passages on pages 174 and 465, omitted in later editions. The author of the work encounters a poor warrior-beggar, an adaptation of Chevalier de St. Louis, and writes verse expressing Yorick’s sentiment that the king and fatherland should not allow a faithful soldier to fall into distress. The work is reviewed in the *Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek*, which acknowledges its pernicious influence and success, noting a perversion of taste in the fatherland. Lessing, regarded as too original and mature, did not follow others slavishly, though he may have drawn on Trim in memory while creating Just.

The likable star got on a stick horse and rode ahead, causing young boys in Germany to gather around him and imitate the horse's speed by breaking sticks from fences and pulling a switch from a bundle of reed. The boys then sat on the sticks and rode behind the likable star, creating a whirlwind that swept everything nearby. This activity, while initially playful among the boys, became widespread as men also joined in, riding with sticks, daggers, and official badges. The whirlwind, which accompanied the likable star, was so intense that if it had remained limited to the young boys, it might have been bearable, but its expansion to include men made it a disruptive and widespread phenomenon.

Sterne includes "Farbenprächtige Schilderungen der ihm ungewohnten sonnenverklärten Landschaft" in the *Sentimental Journey*, which Behmer cites as evidence of Yorick's genuine and pure feeling for nature. However, Sterne provides no detailed descriptions of natural scenery and makes only casual references to it. The well-known passage from *The Familiar Passage* is misinterpreted as showing appreciation of inanimate nature, when it actually criticizes those who fail to find emotional exercise in nature. Thus, Behmer's claim that Sterne understands the beauties of nature is questionable due to the lack of descriptive detail and the passage's true critical intent. The references to nature are repeated in the *Sentimental Journey*, but they do not constitute a sustained or appreciative portrayal of inanimate natural scenery.

The work *Empfindsame Reise der Prinzessin Ananas nach Gros-Glogau*, authored by Gräfin Lichterau and published in Riez in 1798 (page 68), is described as vulgar, revoltingly loathsome, and satirically meanness, serving as an example of low-quality literature masquerading as respectable. A second edition appeared in Manchester in 1798, followed by a London edition in 1812. The translation *Fragmente in Yorick’s Manier*, published in London in 1800 and possibly identical to a 1798 edition, was originally published in 1790 by Kearsley in 12mo and described as a teary contribution to the story of Maria of Moulines. This translation may have been translated by Weisse, though not listed under Goedeke. Laurence Sterne is regarded in Germany as a figure of benign humanity with lavish sympathy for earthly afflictions, becoming a guide, mentor, awakener, and consoler, and serving as a sanction for emotional expression. Yorick is seen as a preceptor, and the *Lorenzodosen* were introduced as an application of Yorick’s teachings to practical human relationships. Percy Fitzgerald authored *The Life of Laurence Sterne*, which is misspelled as "Jonrney" in the bibliography.

Bock, at forty-six years old and no longer youthful, authored *Empfindsame Reise durch die Visitenzimmer am Neujahrstag* (published in 1770 in Cosmopolis), which he described as an unsuccessful imitation of Yorick and Jacobi. The work, also known as *Geschichte eines empfundenen Tages*, features sentimental episodes inspired by Yorick, including a fair peasant-maid weeping by the wayside due to her inability to write, a stern stepfather, an unwelcome suitor, and a lover of her own; Bock gains information about her and comforts her by stroking her cheek and drying her tears, parting with her like brother and sister. Another episode involves an old beggar mourning a dead dog, reflecting a humane movement rooted in Yorick’s dead ass, which Bock directly references and defends warmly. The wanderer’s acquaintance with the lady’s companion is adapted from Yorick’s *fille de chambre*, and Bock includes a fleshly suggestion in Yorick’s style. The *Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek* noted the work’s double inspiration, insufficiency, and tiresomeness. Bock’s next sentimental adventure is with the fair peasant-maid, and the book was criticized as a sentimental journey lacking originality.

Caterpillars are described as part of a natural biological element, often symbolizing transformation or innocence. No specific species, locations, or events are detailed in the provided passages. Their role is primarily symbolic within a broader natural or biological context. No direct connections to other entities are established.

J. C. Bode, born in Braunschweig in 1730, grew up in lowly circumstances and moved to Hamburg in 1756–1757, where he developed a talent for languages and was especially knowledgeable about the English language and literature. He was compared to Yorick in Sterne’s works and published several English translations before 1768, recognizing the adaptability of The Sentimental Journey to German readers. The Sentimental Journey was published in London on February 27, 1768, less than three weeks before the author’s death, and quickly gained influence in Germany, where leaders of thought appreciated its readability while lower-ranking readers could not engage with its complexity. In 1795, a two-volume work titled *Launige Reise durch Holland in Yoricks Manier mit Charakterskizzen und Anekdoten über die Sitten und Gebräuche der Holländer aus dem Englischen* was published in Zittau and Leipzig, written in Yorick’s style and translated from English, including character sketches and anecdotes about Dutch customs. This work is described as a similar product to earlier sentimental journeys. A related travel book, *A Picturesque Tour through Holland, Brabant and part of France*, was made in 1789 and published in London in 1790 in two volumes. The work *Betrachtungen über verschiedene Gegenstände* was published in Braunschweig in 1789.

"Wayward shades of my canvas" refers to unpredictable or erratic elements in the artist's work, indicating a departure from harmony or order in the visual representation. These irregularities are present in the canvas, suggesting a dynamic or chaotic aspect within the artwork. The phrase describes specific visual features that deviate from conventional or balanced composition, contributing to the overall expressive or unconventional nature of the piece.

A work published in Berlin from 1775 to 1780 in nine volumes, with Volume I (1775), Volume II (1775), Volume III (1779), Volume IV (1779), and Volumes V and VI (1780), was reissued in 1778 (Volumes I and II) and 1780 (Volume III). The work was reviewed in *Frankfurter Gel. Anz.* (1775, October 31) and *Allg. Litt.-Zeitung* (1785, Volume V, Supplement-Band, page 80), with a later review in Volume V expressing doubt about it. Lichtenberg criticized Sterne in 1796, referencing Ferriar’s essay *Gelehrte Diebstähle*, claiming Yorick plucked a nettle that grew on Lorenzo’s grave, and made no acknowledgment of Sterne’s extenuating use of borrowings. The author’s compositional difficulties are sketched in a Sterne-derived manner, notably in Chapter IX of Volume III, a lament over chronicling a preceding learned disquisition. Lichtenberg quoted passages from the 1796 *Göttingischer Taschenkalender* and *Vermischte Schriften* (Volume VI, page 487). A separate work, *Auch Vetter Heinrich hat Launen*, is a translation of Beffroy de Regny’s *Les Lunes du Cousin Jacques* by Jünger.

Serenity was wont to fix the state of UNSCULPTED SINS OF THE SENSES, a condition described by the phrase 'Unschuldiges Verbrechen der Sinne,' which contrasts innocence with sensuality. This relationship indicates that serenity previously held a dominant influence, establishing a framework where sensuality, though present, was not dominant. The term reflects a tension between innocence and sensory experience, with serenity acting as a stabilizing force over the unrefined expression of the senses.

Tobias runs away from home and engages in a sentimental adventure involving a so-called soldier’s wife, an episode criticized for bad taste in Yorick’s style. Schummel resumes the original narrative, engaging in a sentimental adventure without imitating Sterne’s diction, introducing an event inspired by Yorick: a meeting with a poor, maimed soldier-beggar. The author encounters a troop of children and responds with unsentimental coldness, revealing the satirical purpose of the narrative. Two maidens, Adelheid and Kunigunde, weep over a dead butterfly and compose a lament, satirizing sentimentalism. The original narrative contained bold indecency, which was softened by substitutions and omissions. Tobias’s sentimental journey is revealed to be a jest created by the Captain, who pranks him with a sentimental journey through the stables, mocking sentimentalism. A review is described as unsympathetic to Timme’s satirical purpose.

Laurence Sterne authored several works, including *The Case of Elijah and the Widow of Zerephath* (preached April 17, 1747, published in York, 1747), *The Abuses of Conscience* (preached July 29, 1750, published in York, 1750), and *The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy*, published in York (1759) and London (1760–1767), with volumes distributed across those years. Sterne also wrote *Sermons of Mr. Yorick*, published in London (1760). Footnote 70 references a passage where a speaker feels dizzy thinking of Elisen’s touch and wishes to be woven with him. Footnote 71 criticizes Sterne for cutting passages from respected writers and combining them absurdly. Goethe turned to Sterne in the 1720s, made quotations from the Koran, and provided translations differing from Bode’s, with Loeper suggesting Goethe translated the quotations himself and being unaware of Gellius’s earlier translation of the Koran, which is actually *Yorick’s Nachgelassene Werke*. A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy (1792, Basel) includes a continuation by Eugenius and an account of Sterne. Footnote 73 notes an error in Loeper’s edition of Hempel (XXII, p. 264), where Gellius is incorrectly credited with translating Lillo and Sterne.

The division of moral preachers into classes is adapted from Sterne and presented in Yorick’s mock-scientific style. Allusions and adaptations reveal a clear demarcation between references to Sterne’s sentimental influence—corresponding to Sterne as an individual—and his whimsical narration and vagaries of thought—corresponding to Sterne as an innovator in literature. The treatment of these two aspects shows a distinct line of cleavage: one side is characterized by exaggerated satirical burlesque, the other by modified, lightened, and softened elements. These two lines of division coincide precisely, indicating a consistent structural and thematic separation in the representation of Sterne’s dual aspects.

Eugenius is a character fancifully styled as Mr. Trim from Shadwell’s *Bury Fair*, and the fragment in Sterne’s work originates directly from this source, not from *Tristram Shandy*. A mistaken association between the fragment and Shandy arose due to the juxtaposition of names linked with Sterne, and those who proposed a connection were unfamiliar with the actual source. Lessing’s Trim shares no commonalities with the Corporal, and no established link exists between the Corporal and Just. Ermindus functions as a kind of Eugenius, serving as a reference, apostrophe, and appeal. The fragment breaks off suddenly, claiming the rest could not be found, mirroring Sterne’s own narrative dependence. Bode adds *Die Erklärung* and its continuations, which unite with the fragment, and alters Eugenius’s chapter *Vendredi-Saint* by changing personnel and introducing a new beginning. A later reference in Wezel’s work touches on pre-birth condition and life’s development, reinforcing thematic links to Sterne’s work.

Schummel is stigmatized as a childish imitator and his book is censured as "beneath criticism," a judgment he later applies to the third volume. He attempted the impossible by adopting another’s "Laune" and produced direct imitations of Sterne, using eccentric orthography, inventing new words, and including emotional conversations and nettle-plucking at the grave. The review, published in the Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek, shows interest in the book despite its frankly unfavorable tone, which is less censorious than the first review. It contains citations of Schummel’s style and notes his imitation of Sterne, reflecting contemporary admiration for Yorick, whose character is described as having a good, emotional heart filled with virtue and moral feeling.

A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy, authored by Mr. Yorick, was published in Göttingen in 1806 by Dietrich, in two books with 271 pages, featuring no introduction or notes. A selection from the "Reliques" was published in Göttingen in 1767, reflecting Germany’s literary outlook that valued worthy, translatable, and reproducible British works, which made the introduction of Yorick almost inevitable. Existing literary relations forecasted and necessitated Yorick’s adoption, though he failed to gain recognition in Germany. Sterne, an English clergyman in a provincial town, was unknown in Germany before Tristram Shandy, with only local fame due to privately circulated and suppressed works. A letter to Raspe, sent from Göttingen on June 2, 1770, was published in Weimarisches Jahrbuch, volume III, page 28. The 1806 edition of Yorick. In Two Books matches the format and page count of the Sentimental Journey.

The third volume of the work, signed April 25, 1772, is critically condemned by its author for much of its content, described as "almost beyond all criticism" and marked by "kläglich, überaus kläglich" whimsical mannerisms, leading the author to believe a reader might discard the entire book. The preacher's opinions in two sections are approved, as are one or two other sections, but the author concludes the first part contains hardly one hundred good pages and that the second part is worse, making him unwilling to examine it further. The volume has little relation to Sterne, though it shares a title connection and the author notes Sterne's "schnurrigt" characterization in a critical section. A spurious third volume was produced in 1760 by John Carr. Schummel wrote the fourth part of Christian Opitz’s novel *Die Gleichheit der menschlichen Herzen*, composed contemporaneously with the third volume, which is praised by the *Magazin der deutschen Critik* for its comedy and is considered the best of the four parts. Schummel’s enthusiasm for Sterne influenced the composition of this work.

His generosity and sensitiveness to human pain, comparable to Yorick’s, manifested when as a boy he would empty his purse into a poor man's bosom. He annually invited neighbors Herr v. and Herr v. to his home every July, engaging in Shandean speculation about trivial relationships. His sermons elevated the vicar of Sutton, and his eccentricities were widely discussed in neighboring parishes and mocked by the cathedral town. His social graces were recognized among county families and in provincial society, with his reputation as a wit spreading beyond the county. In July 1, 1774, he reflected on the 22nd paragraph, which should be read by everyone and is accompanied by typographical eccentricities, discussing trivial relationships involving Herr v. and Herr v. A large red advertisement in the 21st chapter urges readers to skip subsequent pages and start from the 22nd paragraph, containing the phrase "Cuique Suum." The author makes obscure whimsical allusions and includes typographical eccentricities, notably on page I, p. 153.

The Frankfurter Gel. Anz. published reviews on November 27, 1772, and a full analysis of work (1) on April 27, 1773, pages 276–8. It credited Wieland with urging Bode to translate Shandy and noted that selections from related letters were published before their translation in the Englische Allgemeine Bibliothek. The Neue Critische Mitteilungen, published in Greifswald from 1750 to 1807, reviewed Bode’s translation, drawing a parallel with Shakespeare’s work, and was edited by Georg Peter Möller from 1779. The Altonaer Reichs-Postreuter, in an article on June 21, 1773, stated that Holfrath Deinet authored the review. The Teutscher Merkur (1773, II, pp. 228–30) expressed satisfaction that Bode was engaged on Shandy and offered suggestions. Footnote 41 references the earlier publication of selections in the Frankfurter Gel. Anz. (1775, p. 667).

The Mittelstedt translation of the Sentimental Journey, published in 1769 under a slightly altered title, is considered more accurate than Bode’s original work in certain passages and was cited in a review that praised it without knowledge of the original or Bode’s text. This translation triggered a brief controversy between the two translators in contemporary journals. Böttiger first advanced the claim about Bode’s work in his biographical sketch, and it was later repeated by the *Neue Bibl. der schönen Wissenschaften*, Jördens (1806), Danzel-Guhrauer, and Erich Schmidt. Jördens and Hirsching incorrectly state a second edition was published in 1774; Meusel, in his *Lexicon der vom Jahr 1750 bis 1800 verstorbenen teutschen Schriftsteller* (Leipzig, 1816, pp. 472–474), gives the first edition as 1774 and notes an empty date for the second. A 1778 translation titled *Der Koran oder Leben und Meynungen des Tria Juncta in Uno* was attributed to Bode but not listed by Goedeke, Jördens, or Meusel. Parallel passages in the Mittelstedt translation were used to demonstrate Bode’s superiority, though the review lacks critical distinction.

Mme. Medalle compiled and published a collection of letters between Yorick and Eliza, along with a "Fragment in the manner of Rabelais" and an autobiography written specifically for her daughter, Lydia Sterne de Medalle. The collection was first published anonymously in Leipzig in 1776, attributed to Christian Felix Weisse, under the title "Lorenz Sterne’s Briefe an seine vertrautesten Freunde nebst einem Fragment im Geschmack des Rabelais und einer von ihm selbst verfassten Nachricht von seinem Leben und seiner Familie." A Vienna 1797 12mo edition includes the letters between Yorick and Eliza, an appendix of 32 previously unpublished letters, the Rabelais fragment, the "History of a Watchcoat," and explanatory notes. The letters also appear in Nürnberg (1788, 8vo), Vienna (1795, 12mo), and Giessen (1802, German), with J. H. Emmert preparing an explanatory word register for the 1802 edition. Medalle added the Rabelais fragment and the autobiography to her collection, the latter composed for Lydia Sterne de Medalle.

Yorick, a figure associated with Sterne and later with Asmus, conceives of death as a welcome and comfortable presence, depicted as a youth resembling Mercury who calls out to Lorenz and causes the house to waver and split; Yorick drinks from a wreathed cup and embraces death, stating it has no bones and is entirely according to comfort. In Asmus’s "Freund Hein," death is similarly welcomed, and Wilhelm Röseler, citing a 1778 letter, calls Asmus "Germany’s Yorick," though a later correspondent denies Claudius’s resemblance to Sterne. C. F. D. Schubart wrote a poem entitled "Yorick" beginning with "Als Yorik starb, da flog Sein Seelchen auf den Himmel," portraying human fate with gruesomeness and a focus on death and dissolution, reflecting a German view that Sterne was a sympathetic messenger bringing tidings of human weakness to heaven. The poem does not reflect Sterne’s manner. In a separate passage, Strephon rides Yorick’s steed through hills and villages, sings to a youth, and builds up a feeling toward the garden god, who smiles kindly and emits scents, while townspeople flee worries and wish for a carefree life. Two farmsteads in Tyrol are designated as "Nach dem Ideal Yoricks."

Laurence Sterne's career in literature began in 1760 with the publication of the first volumes of *Tristram Shandy*, which were ready for delivery in London that year and achieved immediate fame, marking a personal triumph considered comparable to major literary successes. The *Sermons of Mr. Yorick* were published in 1760 and 1766, and *A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy* appeared in 1768. Sterne's *Watchcoat* story debuted in the first edition of 1769, and other works followed, including *A Political Romance* in 1769. Dr. Edward Young’s *Conjectures on Original Composition*, published in 1759, played a central role in the struggle for originality through reprints, translations, and discussions. *Grandison der Zweite*, written in 1759 and published in 1760, predates *Tristram Shandy* and is noted as an influence on later works. Sterne’s complete works were published in 10 volumes in 1793 and edited by G. E. B. Saintsbury in 1894, both of which were chiefly used in the preparation of later works. Illustrations of Sterne were created by Dr. John Ferriar.

Sterne’s Letters to His Friends on Various Occasions, published in July 1775, contains twelve letters including one by Dr. Eustace and the History of a Watchcoat. One letter, copied from the London Magazine, was translated in the Wandsbecker Bothe (1774) and in the Gothaische Gelehrte Zeitungen (1774, pages 286–287). Prof. Saintsbury accepts only letters Nos. 7, 124 (Dr. Eustace), and 125, while Nos. 4–11 are deemed doubtful, with Nos. 11 and 12 containing lines later included in the standard ten-volume edition. The last letter is likely spurious. The Gothaische Gelehrte Zeitungen, edited by Ettinger and published in Gotha from 1774 to 1804, played a role in disseminating Sterne’s work. Baker, Thomas Stockham, analyzed Sterne’s influence on German literature in Americana Germanica (Vol. II, No. 4, pp. 41–56). Hillebrand’s Deutsche Nationalliteratur seit dem Anfange des achtzehnten Jahrhunderts, published in Hamburg and Gotha in 1850 (2nd edition), covers German national literature from Lessing onward.

In 1772 and 1773, several anonymous travel books were published, each tied to a specific festival: Ostertage, Pfingsttage, Johannistage, and Weynachtstage. These works, based on the Sterne model, feature observations on various subjects, with the first section relating to the festival. Schröder’s Lexicon lists only the Pfingsttage (1772) and Johannistage (1773) under Bock’s name, but evidence from the Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen supports Bock’s authorship of all four. Goedeke does not list any of them. The first volume’s second edition admits the title is derived from Yorick and that it was used due to lack of interest in other travel genres. The title’s description "von einem deutschen Yorick angestellt" is omitted after the first volume. A 1773 translation of Shandy, attributed to Wieland via a forged title page, caused Wieland’s indignant repudiation. Sterne influenced these travel accounts to become more personal, subjective, and humorous, though the actual works fail to deliver on this promise, relying instead on heavy, objective descriptions. The book *Bemerkungen eines Reisenden* includes lines from Gay, promising humor that is not fulfilled. Goedeke implies Opitz authored most parts, but a reviewer argues each part has a different author. A separate 1773 travel work, *Amors Reisen nach Fockzana*, has no connection to Sterne.

"Yorick’s emfindsame Reise durch Frankreich und Italien" was translated by J. J. C. Bode and first published in Hamburg and Bremen in 1768, with subsequent editions in 1769, 1770, 1771, 1772, 1776, 1777, and 1804, and also in Mannheim, Leipzig, and by Rabenhorst. A later edition of "Leben und Meinungen des Tristram Shandy von Sterne" was published in Hannover in 1810, translated by Hahn, and later in Magdeburg in 1831 as part of a collection of humorous foreign novels, volume X, including pages 188, 192, 151, 168, 256, and 257–264, with a section on Laurence Sterne and his works. Another revision of Bode’s work was published in Berlin in 1856, translated by Dr. G. R. Bärmann, and in Leipzig in 1879 as nos. 96–99 of the "Bibliothek ausländischer Klassiker" by F. A. Gelbcke, published by Bibliographisches Institut. A version translated by A. Seubert was published in Leipzig in 1881 by Reclam. A collection of sermons titled "Neue Sammlung von Predigten" was published in Leipzig in 1770 by Hahn, containing sermons by Lorenz Sterne.
